newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislators rebuke Beijing on 1989 crackdown.
newsitem.headline: HK legislators rebuke Beijing on 1989 crackdown.

text.p: Hong Kong legislators rebuked Beijing on Wednesday by overwhelmingly calling on the territory's future sovereign to reverse its condemnation of the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement that it violently suppressed.

But the 29 to one vote supporting pro-democracy legislator Szeto Wah's motion that the student-led protesters should be "vindicated" was purely symbolic, as half the legislative council, mostly pro-China members, boycotted the session.
Szeto regretted that his opponents did not show up.

"When the June 4 incident happened, we went on the street together," he said of one pro-China legislator, recalling the massive street demonstrations that swept Hong Kong in the days after China's military crushed the Beijing protests.
"Our starting point was the same. During the processions when we shouted slogans, he shouted more loudly than me. But when we went on, we went on different paths," he said.

The bloody crackdown on what Beijing called a subversive movement shook confidence in Hong Kong ahead of the British colony's reversion to China. The territory of 6.4 million changes hands at midnight on June 30 this year.

In a vivid reminder of the outrage felt at that time, even in the pro-China camp, pro-democracy activists on Wednesday passed copies of a Beijing-backed newspaper condemning the killing as a "bloody fascist atrocity" to legislators ahead of the vote.

But they were June 5, 1989, editions of the Wen Wei Po, eight years out of date. Dissident staff have long been purged and the paper today toes Beijing's line -- on Tuesday it blasted the Hong Kong government for allowing Chai Ling, a Beijing student leader in 1989, to enter the territory on a visit.

While thousands in Hong Kong still gather on June 4 each year to commemorate the crackdown, the edge has worn off the outrage. Confidence in the territory's post-handover future is high, helped by a robust economy.
"The high-performing economy here is underpinning confidence and social order," said Michael DeGolyer, political analyst at Hong Kong's Baptist University.

With the handover to China 41 days away, Hong Kong's economy is full of good news -- the property market is booming, and the Hang Seng index of blue chip stocks is reaching for record highs on optimism over improved access to the surging Chinese economy.
The son of the man perhaps most responsible for the economic boom and the change in sovereignty, the late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, said on Wednesday he may come to witness the July 1 handover.

Deng Pufang, 53, told reporters in the territory that his father would have deeply regretted not seeing the change of flag and would have liked to "take a walk on Hong Kong soil". The elder Deng died on February 19, aged 92.

Meanwhile, future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa flew to Beijing on Wednesday for talks on foreigners' access to the territory and a threatened influx of mainland immigrants after it reverts to Chinese rule.

Tung will also join a meeting of the China-controlled Preparatory Committee to hammer out the rules for future Hong Kong elections, a sensitive issue as many in Hong Kong fret about the future of their fledgling democratic electoral system.

Most legislators who voted on Wednesday to rebuke Beijing will be unseated on July 1 when the current, elected council is replaced by a provisional body chosen by a Beijing-backed committee. China has promised new polls within a year.
The Joint Liaison Group, the Sino-British diplomatic body overseeing Hong Kong's reversion to China, will meet one more time before the handover, the government said on Wednesday.
On the agenda of the meeting next week will be technical legal issues such as details on the transfer of sentenced persons and procedures for reciprocal enforcement of judgements.
